text: Petra lent her friend Helga 8,000 euros three years ago so Helga could buy a reliable car, with a private written agreement: Helga repays 200 euros a month, interest-free, over 40 months. The agreement includes a clause letting Petra demand full repayment with 30 days' notice if she has an urgent need for the money. Helga still owes 4,800 euros. Petra has just been offered a chance to put 8,000 euros into a friend's small renovation business, which promises a solid return within a year, but she needs the cash now. Calling in the loan would force Helga to scramble, possibly taking a bank loan at high interest, and would strain their friendship, but Petra would be acting within the terms Helga agreed to.
question: Should Petra demand immediate full repayment from Helga?

text: Petra lent her friend Helga 8,000 euros three years ago so Helga could buy a reliable car, with a private written agreement: Helga repays 200 euros a month, interest-free, over 40 months, with no clause allowing early recall under any circumstances. Helga still owes 4,800 euros. Petra has just been offered a chance to put 8,000 euros into a friend's small renovation business, which promises a solid return within a year, but she needs the cash now. Calling in the loan would force Helga to scramble, possibly taking a bank loan at high interest, and would strain their friendship, and doing so would go against the fixed schedule Helga agreed to and relied on.
question: Should Petra demand immediate full repayment from Helga?

text: Michael Berg, 68, practiced law in Cologne for forty years and is now retired. Eleven years ago, a client named Rainer Vogt told him privately, protected by professional confidentiality, that he alone had struck the blow that killed a man in a bar fight in Duisburg. Vogt died three years later without ever being charged. Now Julian Fenn, wrongly suspected at the time, stands before a Cologne court again, retried after new witnesses surfaced, facing a life sentence for that same killing. Berg does not know whether Vogt told him the truth or invented the story to protect his own brother, who was also present that night. German rules on attorney confidentiality generally survive the client's death. Berg could come forward with what Vogt said. Nothing else ties Vogt to the crime.
question: Should Berg disclose Vogt's confession to the court?

text: Priya Nandan runs the licensing unit at a state transport authority. The department has rolled out an automated fraud-detection system for auto-rickshaw permit renewals, flagging applications with mismatched addresses or income inconsistencies. The system flags Suresh, a driver who has renewed his permit for eleven years, because his listed home address doesn't match his bank KYC records. In reality, he moved after his rented room flooded last monsoon and never updated one of the two documents. The system recommends automatic suspension pending a fraud inquiry, which typically takes four to six months, during which he cannot legally operate his vehicle. Priya can override the flag based on his renewal history and issue the permit immediately, or let the automated process run as designed, which was built to stop a genuine wave of forged permits that cost the department crores last year. Suresh earns about 700 rupees a day and has no savings to survive a six-month gap.
question: Should Priya override the system and issue Suresh's permit immediately?

text: Marek manages a twelve-person warehouse team for a distribution company in Wrocław. Yesterday, senior leadership told department heads, in strict confidence, that a restructuring will cut four positions next month, including possibly Tomasz's. Tomasz, one of Marek's best workers, mentioned this morning that he is about to sign a three-year apartment lease costing 2,400 zloty a month and has turned down a job offer from another firm to stay. Marek was told the layoff list is not final and could still change, and leaking it could cost him his own job and expose the company to legal trouble. But if he says nothing, Tomasz may commit to a lease he cannot afford once his income stops. Marek has not been given permission to share anything.
question: Should Marek tell Tomasz that layoffs are coming?

text: Dr. Aris Bakker is the attending physician on call at a regional hospital in Utrecht. His uncle Marten arrives by ambulance with a ruptured appendix and severe internal bleeding, requiring emergency surgery within the hour. Years ago, Aris promised Marten he would personally handle any operation he ever needed, after a previous surgeon's mistake left Marten distrustful of unfamiliar doctors. But Aris has been awake for nineteen hours, his hands are shaking from exhaustion, and hospital protocol requires him to hand off to Dr. Ilse Vermeer, a fully rested surgeon with excellent outcomes, whenever a physician has been on shift this long. Marten, still conscious, begs Aris to keep his promise and operate himself, saying he trusts no one else. Aris knows his fatigue increases the risk of a fatal error, but he feels the weight of his old promise and Marten's fear.
question: Should Aris operate on Marten himself instead of handing off to Dr. Vermeer?

text: The Vila Nova Residents' Association board is deciding whether to grant a street-closure permit exception for a protest planned by a local teachers' union. City rules require organizers to pay 4,000 reais for barricades, security coordination, and cleanup when a demonstration blocks Rua das Palmeiras. The teachers' union, protesting unpaid wages, says it cannot afford the fee and asks the association to waive it, as the association has done twice before for a business chamber event and a religious festival, both of which paid nothing despite the same rules. Board member Otávio Ferreira argues waiving it again invites the city to fine the association for inconsistent enforcement, and some residents will complain about parked cars and noise regardless of who pays. Other members worry refusing looks like the board picking sides against underpaid teachers while wealthier groups got free passes.
question: Should the association grant the teachers' union the same fee waiver it gave the business chamber and the religious festival?

text: Deputy warden Han Seo-yeon reviews the parole file of Lim Ji-tae, an inmate convicted three years ago of embezzling 42 million won from the small logistics company where he worked as an accountant. Lim has a clean disciplinary record, completed vocational training, and shows genuine remorse. His case file also documents a diagnosed gambling disorder that began after his wife's medical bills mounted, a compulsion his psychiatrist argues drove the theft beyond his full control. The victimized company's owner, still not fully repaid, has written a letter opposing early release, calling it an insult to hardworking employees. Releasing Lim now would ease prison overcrowding and let him support his teenage daughter, but it means he serves less than half his original sentence, and the board worries about signaling that financial desperation excuses theft. Han must decide today whether to recommend him.
question: Should Han recommend Lim for parole?

text:
Colonel Arvind Rao heads procurement for a state police department buying bulletproof vests. Eighteen months ago, the department signed a five-year exclusive contract with Suraksha Armour Ltd, promising all vest orders in exchange for a discounted rate of 42,000 rupees per unit and guaranteed supply during shortages. The contract has held up well; Suraksha delivered reliably during a difficult year.

Now a newer firm, Kavach Defence Systems, offers vests independently certified to stop rounds the current model cannot, at 38,000 rupees per unit. Two constables were shot last month wearing Suraksha vests that failed against a criminal gang's upgraded weapons; both survived but with permanent injuries. Kavach cannot guarantee supply volumes yet, and breaking the contract exposes the department to legal penalties and may damage trust with future vendors who rely on government contracts being honored.
question: Should Colonel Rao cancel the Suraksha contract and switch immediately to Kavach vests?

text: Rutger de Groot runs a mid-sized construction firm in Rotterdam that installs prefabricated balconies on apartment towers. A structural engineer flags that eleven balconies installed three years ago, using a batch of steel brackets from a now-defunct supplier, show slightly more corrosion than expected for their age. The engineer recommends a full inspection of all 340 balconies from that era, costing 190,000 euros and requiring residents to vacate their balconies for six weeks. Rutger commissions an independent metallurgical study. The study finds the corrosion pattern matches a labeling error: the "affected" brackets were actually a later, better-treated batch, and the original batch performs within spec. Load tests on ten sampled brackets from the true original batch show no measurable weakness. Rutger's board notes the study cost 40,000 euros and closes the file, ready to move on without notifying residents or ordering further checks.
question: Should Rutger de Groot close the file without notifying residents or ordering further checks?

text: Rutger de Groot runs a mid-sized construction firm in Rotterdam that installs prefabricated balconies on apartment towers. A structural engineer flags that eleven balconies installed three years ago, using a batch of steel brackets from a now-defunct supplier, show slightly more corrosion than expected for their age. The engineer recommends a full inspection of all 340 balconies from that era, costing 190,000 euros and requiring residents to vacate their balconies for six weeks. Rutger commissions an independent metallurgical study. The study confirms the brackets from that batch were improperly galvanized and are corroding faster than spec allows. Load tests on ten sampled brackets show measurable strength loss, with two failing well below the safety margin. Rutger's board notes the study cost 40,000 euros and that a recall would draw negative press and strain cash flow, and considers closing the file without notifying residents or ordering further checks.
question: Should Rutger de Groot close the file without notifying residents or ordering further checks?

text: Ramesh Oswal is the District Education Officer for a block in Madhya Pradesh. An anonymous complaint reaches his desk about Mr. Damodar Pillai, a government school teacher two months from retirement. Eleven years ago, Pillai wrote a recommendation letter for a student applying to a railway apprenticeship, describing the boy as having topped his class in mathematics when his actual rank was ninth. The student got the position and has since supported his family on the salary. Oswal confirms the discrepancy in old records. Formal rules require he report the falsification, which would trigger an inquiry, likely stripping Pillai of his pension of about 14,000 rupees a month and his retirement gratuity. Oswal knows many teachers write similarly generous letters and are never checked, and Pillai's record is otherwise clean. The complainant, a rival teacher passed over for a promotion, has clear motives of his own.
question: Should Oswal formally report Pillai's letter as academic fraud?

text: Marcus Tan chairs the credit committee at a government-backed lending board in Singapore that provides emergency working-capital loans to small manufacturers during supply shocks. A dam-related flood has shut down four industrial estates, and 60 firms have applied for the board's last S$8 million tranche this quarter, far exceeding available funds. One applicant, Hin Leong Precision, is run by his university roommate Desmond, who employs 140 workers building components for medical ventilators; the factory floor is underwater and payroll is due in nine days. Desmond's application is technically complete but arrived after the published cutoff because his office internet was down. Other late applicants, including one firm supplying similar ventilator parts, were rejected on the same grounds. Approving Desmond's loan would mean redirecting funds earmarked for on-time applicants ranked higher by the board's scoring model, some of whom also face payroll deadlines and layoffs affecting hundreds of workers. Marcus can quietly instruct staff to accept Desmond's late file as an exception.
question: Should Marcus accept Desmond's late application as an exception to the cutoff rule?

text: Deputy Public Prosecutor Mei Ling Tan is preparing for the trial of a man accused of running a home renovation racket that took deposits from elderly clients and vanished, leaving one victim, a 78-year-old widow, so distressed she suffered a stroke. Tan has a strong case built on bank records and testimony. Her chief witness, a former employee named Farid, has agreed to testify against the accused, but he privately admits to Tan that he lied about one detail: he claims he saw the accused shred documents, when in fact he only heard about it secondhand. Farid says the rest of his testimony is true and the lie is small compared to the harm the accused caused. Tan worries that without this vivid detail, the jury may doubt Farid's credibility, and the accused could walk free to target more victims. Trial begins in three days.
question: Should Tan let Farid testify to the shredding detail as though he witnessed it himself?

text: Marina Costa, secretary of health for a mid-sized city in Pernambuco, must decide whether to approve citywide deployment of an automated ambulance-dispatch system after a six-month pilot. The system cut average response times by 22 percent and saved the department 400,000 reais in dispatcher costs. But an internal audit flagged that calls from Vila Esperança, a poor neighborhood, received priority scores 15 percent lower than the citywide average, raising fears the algorithm undervalues calls from poorer areas. Marina orders an independent review. Statisticians find the gap disappears once they control for reported symptom severity and call duration; the lower scores simply reflected genuinely less urgent calls that period, not neighborhood bias. Some staff still worry the sample was too small to be sure. Marina must decide before the funding window closes.
question: Should Marina Costa approve citywide deployment of the automated dispatch system?

text: Marina Costa, secretary of health for a mid-sized city in Pernambuco, must decide whether to approve citywide deployment of an automated ambulance-dispatch system after a six-month pilot. The system cut average response times by 22 percent and saved the department 400,000 reais in dispatcher costs. But an internal audit flagged that calls from Vila Esperança, a poor neighborhood, received priority scores 15 percent lower than the citywide average, raising fears the algorithm undervalues calls from poorer areas. Marina orders an independent review. Statisticians confirm the gap persists even after controlling for symptom severity, call duration, and time of day: the training data underweighted certain accents and word choices common in that neighborhood, causing real calls to be misclassified as less urgent. Fixing the model would take months. Marina must decide before the funding window closes.
question: Should Marina Costa approve citywide deployment of the automated dispatch system?

text: Lars manages a logistics team of twelve at a distribution center outside Malmö. Head office orders a cut of two positions, based on seniority and performance scores. The lowest scorer is Mikael, Lars's childhood friend who vouched for him years ago when Lars was jobless and struggling, even lending him 15,000 kronor without asking when it would be repaid. Mikael has been slower since his divorce, missing small targets, while a newer employee, Farida, consistently outperforms him but has no such history with Lars. Company policy lets managers weigh "extenuating circumstances" in borderline cases, and Lars could cite Mikael's personal difficulties to shift the cut to someone else, a quieter employee named Petra whose numbers are only slightly better than Mikael's. Petra has no idea any of this is happening. Lars knows the review board rarely questions these calls.
question: Should Lars adjust the performance scores to protect Mikael from the layoff?

text: The board of Foyer Sainte-Marguerite, a small elder-care residence in Annecy, meets to decide whether to report a broken fire-suppression system in the west wing. Director Colette Vasseur discovered the fault during an inspection: the sprinkler line has been disconnected since a renovation eight months ago, and reconnecting it will cost 42,000 euros the foyer does not have. Reporting the defect to the regional safety authority will trigger an immediate closure order for that wing until repairs are made, forcing the relocation of eleven elderly residents, some with dementia, to other facilities during peak winter demand. Staff worry the disruption could harm frail residents, and the board fears the foyer's reputation and finances may not survive the closure. Colette knows French law requires disclosure of such hazards, and that a fire in an unsprinklered wing could kill residents who cannot evacuate themselves. Some board members argue they can quietly fix it within a month without reporting.
question: Should the board report the fire-suppression failure to the regional safety authority immediately?

text: Marieke lives on a quiet street in Utrecht, three doors from a city council member, Dhr. Bakker, whose vote next week will approve a new bus depot behind her row of houses. She has learned, through a leaked planning memo a neighbor forwarded by mistake, that Bakker owns a small stake in the construction firm awarded the contract. Publishing this online would likely trigger a formal inquiry and could sink the depot project, protecting her home's value and her street's quiet. But the memo was clearly not meant for her, and passing it to a journalist could expose the neighbor who forwarded it by accident, costing that neighbor his city hall job and possibly a defamation suit if the conflict-of-interest claim doesn't hold up. Marieke has saved the file on her laptop and a reporter has already asked her, directly, if she has anything.
question: Should Marieke send the leaked memo to the reporter?

text: Camille Fabron is a parole board magistrate in Lyon reviewing the file of Denis Ory, convicted three years ago of embezzling 90,000 euros from an elderly client while working as a notary's clerk. Ory has served the minimum term, completed every program offered, and his psychological evaluation is strong. He has a job waiting at his brother-in-law's logistics firm. The victim, now in a care home, has recovered only 12,000 euros and will never see the rest. Ory's lawyer argues the man was a first-time offender under crushing debt from his mother's medical bills, and that further detention serves no purpose. Camille is tired after a long docket of harder cases, and approving the file quickly would let her leave for her daughter's recital. Nothing in Ory's record or evaluation gives her genuine grounds for concern.
question: Should Camille approve Denis Ory's parole?

text: Erik Malmgren runs a two-person consultancy in Umeå and wants a spot on the approved supplier list for the municipality's building maintenance contracts, worth roughly 400,000 kronor a year. The application asks whether the company has completed projects of similar scale in the past three years. Erik's firm has completed one such project, finished eighteen months ago for a housing cooperative, well documented and successful. The form's wording, "projects" plural, technically doesn't fit his single case, but nothing requires he name a number, and he can phrase his answer to describe the project in ways that reasonably suggest a broader track record without stating a false number outright. A rival firm with weaker actual performance but more listed contracts is likely to win the slot otherwise. Erik has bills coming due and no other major contract in sight. He believes his work quality matches or beats the competition.
question: Should Erik phrase his application to imply multiple comparable projects when he has completed only one?

text: Priya owns a duplex in Hamilton and rents the lower unit to the Okafor family, who have never missed a payment in three years. Under Ontario law, a landlord can evict a tenant to move in a close family member, and Priya's mother wants to live closer to her grandchildren. Priya's cousin Denise, who has no intention of moving in, offers Priya $4,000 cash to file the same kind of eviction notice against her own tenant, a single father named Marcus, so Denise's boyfriend can quietly take over the unit at a higher rent once Marcus leaves. Denise says no one will ever check, and $4,000 would cover Priya's property tax bill this year. Priya knows the "bad faith" eviction is illegal and that tenant boards rarely investigate unless the tenant complains, and Marcus has never mentioned knowing his rights. Priya could use the money, and Denise is family.
question: Should Priya file the bad-faith eviction notice against Marcus in exchange for the $4,000?

text: Mr. Cronin teaches final-year business studies at a secondary school in Waterford. One of his students, Aidan, is applying for a university scholarship worth 4,000 euros a year, money his family badly needs since his father lost his job. Aidan asks Mr. Cronin to write a reference and, almost as an afterthought, mentions that the form asks whether the student has ever been disciplined for academic dishonesty. Aidan was caught copying an essay eighteen months ago and given a formal warning, recorded in his file. He asks Mr. Cronin to simply tick "no" on the form, explaining that one mistake shouldn't ruin his only chance at college, and that no one will ever check. Mr. Cronin likes Aidan and believes he has genuinely changed. The form requires Mr. Cronin's signature confirming the answer is accurate.
question: Should Mr. Cronin tick "no" on the form?

text: Kenji Otani directs emergency loan relief at a regional development bank in Niigata after a landslide destroys forty homes. The board approved a disaster relief fund of 500 million yen, with a public promise that affected households would receive interest-free bridge loans within two weeks so they can rebuild before winter snow makes construction impossible. Now, three days before disbursement, Kenji discovers a clerical rule requiring each applicant's property title to be re-verified by the land registry, a process that normally takes six weeks. His compliance officer insists the rule cannot be waived without board approval, and the board chair is unreachable at a conference. Families are already sleeping in gymnasiums, and a delay risks leaving them without shelter before the first snowfall, which local officials warn could cause deaths among elderly residents. Kenji can approve the loans now based on existing tax records and photographs, documenting the exception for later board review, or he can wait for full verification as the rule requires.
question: Should Kenji approve the loans now without completing the registry re-verification?

text: Nils Holmberg is a defense attorney in Malmö representing a client accused of embezzling from a small logistics firm. While reviewing files the prosecution disclosed, he finds a spreadsheet showing the company's accountant, not his client, moved the missing 340,000 kronor, then quietly restored part of it. The prosecution seems not to have noticed this detail buried in a larger dataset. If Nils raises it, his client is likely acquitted, but the case will drag on for months as the court investigates the accountant, delaying payment of his fee and creating awkwardness with the prosecutor's office, which he works with often. If he stays quiet and lets the trial proceed on the existing evidence, his client will probably still be convicted, but the case will close quickly and cleanly.
question: Should Nils disclose the spreadsheet finding to the court?

text: Mei Lin runs a small credit-assessment consultancy in Singapore, using a machine-learning model she licensed from a vendor to score loan applicants for a client bank. The model flags a young hawker-stall owner, Farah, as high risk, largely because Farah's postal code correlates with past defaults. Mei Lin has discretion to override the score for individual cases before submitting her report, but overrides must be justified in writing and are periodically audited by the bank's compliance team. She has met Farah, reviewed her actual repayment history and steady cash flow, and believes the model is picking up neighborhood bias rather than real risk. Overriding could help Farah get a $40,000 loan to keep her stall running. But Mei Lin's contract renewal depends on her override rate staying low and matching the model's predictions closely, and too many overrides could cost her the contract that supports her own family.
question: Should Mei Lin override the model's score for Farah?

text: Miriam Ashworth is finance director at a regional NHS trust facing a £1.4 million shortfall this year. Two services must share the cut: the community stroke rehabilitation team, which helps around 400 patients a year avoid permanent disability, and the district minor injuries unit, which treats roughly 3,000 people annually for cuts, sprains and fractures. Closing either team's shortfall through redundancies would meet the target; the trust's own data on long-term outcomes for both services is incomplete, and consultants disagree on which cut would cause more harm. Miriam's closest friend, Elaine, leads the stroke rehabilitation team and has told her privately that losing three staff would likely force the service to close entirely. No one else on the board knows about the friendship. Miriam must recommend one unit for the full reduction by Friday.
question: Should Miriam recommend cutting the minor injuries unit's funding instead of the stroke rehabilitation team's?

text: Wei Han directs flood operations for the national water agency during a week of record rainfall. Sensors show the Kallang Reservoir dam is minutes from structural failure; if it breaks, a wall of water will hit a densely populated valley within twenty minutes, likely killing residents who have no time to evacuate. The only way to relieve pressure is to open the floodgates now, which will send water into a lower industrial area first, destroying his brother-in-law Teck Guan's warehouse and its $600,000 stock of goods. Wei Han had promised Teck Guan weeks earlier that he would always give him advance notice before any planned discharge, so the family could move inventory. There is no time to call him now without further delaying the release, and every minute increases the risk to the valley below.
question: Should Wei Han order the floodgates opened immediately?

text: The Residents' Welfare Association of Meadow Enclave, a gated community in Pune, holds an emergency meeting after the district administration denies permission for a planned protest march past their gate, citing traffic safety. The organizer, a local labor union, has complied and rerouted the march through a public road half a kilometer away, still audible from the colony. Association president Ravindra Deshmukh proposes hiring forty men to block the alternate road with parked cars and garbage trucks, making the reroute impossible and forcing the marchers to disperse. He argues the union has caused their colony "enough trouble already" and that spending eighteen thousand rupees on this will save residents from noise and embarrassment in front of visiting relatives during a wedding season. Several members worry this obstructs a lawful, permitted march and could trap emergency vehicles and pedestrians on that public road.
question: Should the association pay to block the public road to stop the permitted march?

text: Marek Tuszyński has worked as a warehouse supervisor at Bronex Logistics in Wrocław for eleven years. Six months ago he was diagnosed with a seizure disorder triggered by stress, confirmed by two neurologists. Three weeks ago, during an unwitnessed episode, he fell against a loaded pallet rack, and it collapsed onto a colleague, breaking her arm and crushing two fingers. Medical records confirm the seizure was involuntary. Company policy requires dismissal after any safety incident causing injury, regardless of cause, to preserve the plant's safety certification and insurance rates. Marek's union representative argues that firing a man for an event his body forced on him is not discipline but punishment for being sick, and that with medication his seizures are now controlled. The injured colleague, Ilona, says she does not blame him but is afraid to work near him again. Losing this job would end Marek's pension eligibility, three years short, at fifty-eight.
question: Should Bronex Logistics dismiss Marek?
